column2: On the authority of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) said:

“Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent; whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour; and whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
Yuʾminu (“believes”): with complete faith, which saves from the punishment of Allah and leads to His pleasure.
Bi-llāh (“in Allah”): that He is the One who created him.
Wa-l-yawm al-ākhir (“and the Last Day”): that he will be recompensed for his deeds on it.
Fa-l-yaqul (“let him speak”): this lām is the lām of command; it may take sukūn or kasrah because it comes after fāʾ.

Khayran (“good”): such as conveying from Allah and from His Messenger, teaching good, commanding what is right with knowledge and forbearance and forbidding what is wrong with knowledge and gentleness, reconciling between people, speaking well to them, and a word of truth before someone whose evil is feared and whose good is hoped for, with steadfastness and good intention.
Li-yaṣmut (“remain silent”): with ḍammah or kasrah on the mīm; let him keep quiet.
“Let him honour his neighbour”: by being kind to him, keeping harm away from him, bearing with what comes from him, showing him a cheerful face, and other ways of honouring.
“Let him honour his guest”: by showing him a cheerful face, speaking pleasantly with him and offering what is readily available.
A warning against the faults of the tongue: a person should think about what he wants to say; if it is clear to him that there is no harm to him in saying it, he says it,

and if it is clear to him that there is harm in it, or he is in doubt about it, he refrains. The Lawgiver has recommended refraining from many permissible things, lest they drag one into what is unlawful or disliked.
Making known the right of the neighbour, and urging that one guard his neighbourly rights and honour him. In explaining this honouring it has come from him ﷺ that he said:

“If he asks you for a loan, lend to him; if he asks your help, help him; if he falls ill, visit him; if he is in need, give to him; if he becomes poor, return to him [with help]; if good befalls him, congratulate him;
if calamity befalls him, console him; if he dies, follow his funeral; do not build higher than him so as to block the wind from him, except with his permission;

do not annoy him with the smell of your cooking pot unless you ladle some out for him; if you buy fruit, give him some as a gift, and if you do not, bring it in secretly, and do not let your child take it out to annoy his child with it.”
In some of its narrations: “and if he is destitute, clothe him.” The chains of this hadith are very weak, but the variety of their sources suggests that it has some basis (Fatḥ al-Bārī).
The command to honour the guest, which is among the manners of Islam and the character of the prophets.
These qualities are among the branches of faith,
which is evidence that deeds are included in faith.
The qualities mentioned in the hadith come down to ridding oneself of vice and adorning oneself with virtue.
